parsed_answer.content: A WeakHashMap in Java is a specialized, concurrency-unfriendly implementation of the java.util.Map interface that uses weak references for its keys. Unlike a standard HashMap where keys are held via strong references—forcing the Garbage Collector to retain them in the JVM heap as long as the map itself is reachable—a WeakHashMap allows its keys to be garbage-collected when no other strong references to those keys exist in the application. This core capability prevents memory leaks in scenarios where external objects need to be dynamically associated with transient metadata. When a key is collected, its corresponding entry is automatically removed from the map during subsequent mutation or accessor operations, mediated via an internal ReferenceQueue.

items: WeakHashMap relies heavily on the java.lang.ref.WeakReference class and a shared ReferenceQueue. When keys lose all strong references, the garbage collector enqueues them into this queue.
The map periodically polls this ReferenceQueue during normal operations (like get(), put(), or size()) to purge stale entries whose keys have already been finalized and collected.
Because it is not synchronized, wrapping it via Collections.synchronizedMap() is mandatory in multithreaded environments, though external synchronization is still required for compound operations.
Values in a WeakHashMap are held via strong references. If a value strongly references its own key, a memory leak will occur because the key will never become weakly reachable.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of the 'Value Strong Reference Trap': if your WeakHashMap's value object contains a reference (direct or indirect) back to its key, the key will remain strongly reachable, completely defeating the purpose of the WeakHashMap and causing a subtle, persistent memory leak.
